sections.history: Ahobilam lies in Nandyal district of Andhra Pradesh, where Thirumangai Alvar sang the lord of Singavel Kundram, the lion-hill, in a decad of ten verses in the Periya Thirumozhi. It is one of the 108 Divya Desams, the abodes of Vishnu praised by the Alvars in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and belongs to Vada Nadu, the northern region of the tradition. The Vijayanagara rulers patronised the shrines, first the Saluva dynasty in the fifteenth century and then the Tuluva dynasty in the sixteenth, and Krishnadevaraya is remembered as a visitor and benefactor. Ahobila Matha, the Sri Vaishnava monastic institution, took shape here in the medieval period. The story of the hills before the sixteenth century is largely obscure, and the Alvar's hymn remains the surest voice of their antiquity.
sections.architecture: Ahobilam is not a single temple but a pilgrimage of shrines scattered through the hills. The principal shrine is Upper Ahobilam, where Ahobila, or Ugra, Narasimha is worshipped, and around it the tradition counts the Nava Narasimha: Bhargava, Yogananda, Chatravata, Karanja, Pavana, Malola, Varaha (Kroda) and Jvala Narasimha. Below, in Lower Ahobilam, stands the Prahladavarada temple of Lakshmi Narasimha, regarded as a separate and later shrine. A crag called Ugra Stambham is pointed out as the pillar from which the Lord appeared. To reach the hill shrines is to climb, and the climb is part of the offering.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells that Vishnu burst from a pillar as Narasimha, half man and half lion, to destroy the tyrant Hiranyakashipu and protect his young devotee Prahlada. Tradition holds that the watching gods cried 'Aho balam!' — 'what strength!' — and so the place took its name. The hill is also called Garudadri after the penance of Garuda, and tradition tells that Narasimha here wed Chenchu Lakshmi, a daughter of the forest-dwelling Chenchu people, so that the fierce lord of the hills is also the kinsman of the people who live in them.
sections.festivals: The shrines keep an annual Brahmotsavam, and Narasimha Jayanti is a day of special worship. After Sankranti, tradition has the Lord carried in procession to the Chenchu villages in the Paruveta festival, recalling his bond with the hill people. Vaikunta Ekadashi is observed as at other Divya Desams. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Come prepared for a pilgrimage rather than a visit: the shrines are spread across forested hills, and the walk between them is long and often steep. Wear sturdy footwear for the paths, carry water, and allow more than a day if you hope to see several of the nine. Upper Ahobilam is the heart of the journey.

visit.timings: Shrines are open daily with morning and evening darshan sessions and a midday closure; festival days are busiest, and the hill shrines may be reached only in daylight. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear removed before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is restricted in and around the sanctum; follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Ahobilam lies in Nandyal district (formerly part of Kurnool district), reached by road via Allagadda; Nandyal is the nearest major railhead. Upper and Lower Ahobilam and the hill shrines are reached by local road transport and on foot; confirm routes locally.
